title: Episode 233: Greece: Thermopylae and Salamis: King Leonidas, Themistocles, and the Persian Defeat

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, we stand upon the narrow mountain passes and churning coastal waters of ancient Greece to witness one of the most celebrated struggles for human freedom in world history: King Leonidas at Thermopylae and Themistocles at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE PERSIAN COLOSSUS AND THE WRATH OF XERXES
In the spring of 480 BC, the Great King of Persia, Xerxes, son of Darius, assembled the largest invasion force the ancient world had ever witnessed, marching across the Hellespont into Europe to avenge the Persian defeat at Marathon ten years earlier and reduce the independent city-states of Greece to imperial provinces. Xerxes commanded an immense multi-ethnic armada of over one thousand warships and an army numbering in the hundreds of thousands—Persian Immortals, Median spearmen, Assyrian charioteers, and Nubian archers whose marching boots shook the earth. According to Herodotus, the Persian host drank entire rivers dry as they advanced. Confronted with this terrifying juggernaut, Greek city-states trembled; many medized, surrendering soil and water in tokens of submission to Persian heralds. Only a fragile confederation of thirty-one Greek cities, led by the military powerhouse of Sparta and the maritime democracy of Athens, resolved to stand their ground, pledging to defend Greek liberty or perish together.  To cross the Hellespont, Xerxes's engineers lashed nearly seven hundred Phoenician and Egyptian galleys together with thick papyrus cables, constructing two massive floating pontoon bridges paved with brushwood and packed earth.  Xerxes's imperial pontoon bridge across the Hellespont was destroyed by a sudden autumn storm, prompting the Great King to order the waters of the strait scourged with three hundred lashes and branded with hot irons.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE HOT GATES: THE NARROW PASS OF THERMOPYLAE
To halt the Persian advance into central Greece, the allied Greeks selected the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae—the 'Hot Gates', named for its steaming sulfurous springs—where the steep cliffs of Mount Kallidromos plunged directly into the waters of the Malian Gulf. At its narrowest point, the pass was barely fifty feet wide, an ideal defensive choke-point where Xerxes's overwhelming numerical superiority would be completely negated. Command of the pass was entrusted to the sixty-year-old King of Sparta, Leonidas, of the royal Agiad dynasty. Because Sparta was celebrating the sacred religious festival of the Carneia, which forbade full military mobilization, Leonidas departed with an elite royal bodyguard of just three hundred veteran Spartan hoplites—each a father who had already fathered a living son to carry on his family name. Arriving at the pass, the three hundred Spartans were joined by approximately seven thousand allied Peloponnesians, Thespians, and Phocians, rebuilding an ancient stone Phocian wall across the defile and bracing for the Persian assault.  The pass of Thermopylae was dominated by the rugged cliffs of Mount Kallidromos on the south and treacherous coastal marshes on the north, preventing the massive Persian cavalry from deploying on the field.  The Phocian wall at Thermopylae had been constructed by local Greek villagers to defend their sulfurous springs from northern raiders, its crumbling stone blocks hastily repaired by Leonidas's hoplites before the battle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: 'MOLON LABE': THE FIRST TWO DAYS OF SLAUGHTER
When Xerxes arrived at Thermopylae, his scouts observed the Spartans outside the wall casually exercising and combing their long hair, which Xerxes interpreted as childish vanity. His advisor Demaratus, an exiled Spartan king, warned him: 'These men have come to fight for the pass, and they are preparing their long hair to face death with honor.' Xerxes sent a herald demanding that the Greeks surrender their weapons; Leonidas shouted back his immortal, laconic reply: 'Molon labe'—'Come and take them!' When a Persian envoy sneered that Persian archers were so numerous their arrows would blot out the sun, the Spartan Dieneces laughed: 'All the better; we shall fight in the shade!' For two full days, Xerxes threw wave after wave of Medes, Cissians, and his elite royal bodyguards, the Ten Thousand Immortals, into the pass. Armed with short daggers, wicker shields, and light spears, the Persians were systematically slaughtered by the interlocking bronze shields, heavy iron-tipped ash spears, and disciplined phalanx formations of the heavily armored Greek hoplites, piling up thousands of dead before the Spartan wall.  Dieneces's sharp wit and unyielding courage became the defining ethos of the Spartan warrior code, celebrating death in defense of the homeland as the highest honor a man could achieve in life.  The Spartan shield, or aspis, was a massive circular bowl of wood faced with thin bronze and lined with leather, weighing sixteen pounds and engineered to lock with neighboring shields in an impenetrable bronze wall.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TREASON OF EPHIALTES AND THE FINAL STAND
On the evening of the second day, Xerxes's despair turned to triumph when a local Malian Greek shepherd named Ephialtes entered the Persian camp, seeking gold and glory by betraying his countrymen. Ephialtes revealed the existence of the secret Anopaia mountain trail that bypassed the cliffs and emerged behind the Greek position at Thermopylae. Under cover of darkness, Hydarnes led the Immortals over the pine-clad heights, brushing aside the Phocian defenders. At dawn, lookouts ran to Leonidas warning that the Persians were surrounding them from the rear. Leonidas dismissed the allied Greek contingents to save them to fight another day, but he and his three hundred Spartans, joined by seven hundred brave Thespians under Demophilus who refused to abandon them, prepared for their final stand. Knowing they were doomed, the Greeks advanced into the wider part of the pass to maximize the slaughter of the enemy. Leonidas fell in the fighting, and a ferocious struggle ensued over his corpse. When their spears broke, the Spartans fought with short swords, and when their swords shattered, they fought with bare hands and teeth, until the last warriors were overwhelmed by a shower of Persian arrows.  The Thespians under Demophilus chose to remain with Leonidas out of pure patriotic honor, refusing to save their own lives when their fellow Greeks were about to perish on the field of sacrifice.  Demophilus and his seven hundred Thespians demonstrated that devotion to freedom was not the exclusive monopoly of Sparta's martial elite, giving their lives willingly to buy time for the Greek coalition to escape.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BURNING OF ATHENS AND THE WOODEN WALLS OF SALAMIS
With the pass of Thermopylae broken, the Persian army flooded into Attica. In Athens, panic reigned as citizens recalled the enigmatic prophecy of the Delphic Oracle: 'Though all else be taken, Zeus grants to Athena that a wooden wall alone shall remain uncaptured, a boon to you and your children.' While some citizens mistakenly barricaded themselves behind wooden palisades on the Acropolis, the visionary Athenian naval commander Themistocles interpreted the 'wooden wall' as the newly constructed fleet of two hundred Athenian triremes—the fastest, most agile oared warships in the Mediterranean. Themistocles evacuated the entire civilian population of Athens across the water to the island of Salamis and Troezen. Looking back from their ships, Athenian families wept as they saw smoke billowing into the sky: Xerxes had occupied the deserted city, sacking and burning the Acropolis and the ancient temple of Athena to ashes.  The Athenian trireme was propelled by one hundred and seventy skilled oarsmen sitting in three staggered tiers, rowing in perfect unison to the rhythm of an aulos flute player to accelerate the ship to nine knots.  The trireme's hull was constructed using intricate mortise-and-tenon joinery, creating a light, flexible wooden structure that could withstand the violent shock of ramming enemy warships at full rowing speed.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE RUSE OF THEMISTOCLES: THE TRAP AT SALAMIS
The Greek naval commanders were gripped by panic: Spartan admiral Eurybiades and the Peloponnesian captains insisted on sailing south to defend the Isthmus of Corinth, which would have dissolved the coalition and doomed Greece. Seeing that the allied fleet would scatter, Themistocles performed an act of breathtaking psychological espionage. On the night of September 28, 480 BC, he dispatched his trusted Persian slave, Sicinnus, in a rowing boat to Xerxes's camp with a secret message: 'The Athenian commander is your friend and wishes you victory; the Greeks are terrified and preparing to flee in the night; if you block the straits now, you can destroy them all at once.' Xerxes took the bait: he ordered his massive armada of eight hundred ships into the narrow, constricted channel between Salamis and the Attic mainland, rowing through the night to seal the exits. The Persian captains were exhausted, while their massive ships were crammed into a bottleneck where their numerical superiority was utterly useless.  Themistocles's messenger Sicinnus was so convincing that Xerxes rewarded him with gold before ordering his captains to embark on the ill-fated night operation into the Salamis channel.  Themistocles's calculated deception of Xerxes demonstrated his extraordinary strategic audacity, using the Great King's own imperial hubris and overconfidence as the ultimate weapon of Persian destruction.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TRIUMPH OF THE TRIREMES AND THE DELIVERANCE OF GREECE
At dawn on September 29, 480 BC, Xerxes sat upon a golden throne erected on the slopes of Mount Aigaleo overlooking the strait, surrounded by scribes ready to record his captains' heroic deeds. Instead, he witnessed an unmitigated slaughter. As the morning trumpet sounded, the Greek triremes surged forward in perfect formation, their crews singing the holy battle paean: 'O sons of the Greeks, advance! Free your fatherland, free your children, your wives, the shrines of your gods, and the tombs of your ancestors! Today is the struggle for all!' Using their bronze battering rams at the waterlines, the agile Greek triremes sheared off the oars of the heavy Phoenician and Persian galleys, ramming into their hulls and capsizing them in the crowded waters. Ships collided in blind panic; Queen Artemisia of Halicarnassus escaped only by ramming one of her own allied Persian ships. Over three hundred Persian warships were sunk or captured. Xerxes, terrified that the Greeks would sail north to destroy his pontoon bridge across the Hellespont, fled back to Asia with the bulk of his army. The following spring, allied Greek hoplites annihilated the remaining Persian army at Plataea, securing the freedom of Greece and preserving the nascent civilization of the West.  As the Persian fleet broke in panic, Athenian hoplites landed on the small islet of Psyttaleia, wiping out Xerxes's elite noble infantry who had been stationed there to slaughter shipwrecked Greeks.  The victory at Salamis preserved the fledgling democracy of Athens from imperial annihilation, creating the secure maritime environment that enabled the classical flowering of Western philosophy, art, and science.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our European journey moves north to the soaring alpine peaks of Switzerland with Episode 236: Switzerland Part 1—William Tell, the Apple Shot at Altdorf, and the Oath of the Rütli. Until then, stay curious.
